metadata.method: Evidence-first review of dated primary sources and cross-institution corroboration, with original candidate provenance and claim/rights gates preserved.

reviews.title_after: Dense valley fog triggers a massive Highway 58 pileup near Bakersfield
reviews.location_after: State Route 58 near Caliente, southeast of Bakersfield, California
reviews.evidence_independence: Contemporaneous independent newsroom recount of the same California highway crashes; original NCEI entry and reporting likely both rely on highway-patrol records, not independent visibility instrumentation
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: On January 3, 2002, intense fog around the Tehachapi foothills on State Route 58 near Bakersfield coincided with a major chain-reaction traffic collision.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Contemporary reports vary between 77 and 78 involved vehicles, and some distinguish eastbound and westbound collisions. Verify final California Highway Patrol count, crash sequence, injuries, and fog visibility from dated observations before publishing numerical claims.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original State Route 58 Caliente corridor map and low-cloud/fog satellite–surface observation timeline; do not reproduce newspaper photos

reviews.title_after: A Washington snowstorm exposes deadly aviation icing risks in Flight 90 crash
reviews.location_after: Washington National Airport and Potomac River, Washington, D.C.
reviews.evidence_independence: NTSB independent technical investigation and Smithsonian's separate institutional record of DC snowstorm and tragedy; Smithsonian is not an independent NTSB aerodynamic analysis
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: Washington, D.C. was affected by snow on January 13, 1982, when Air Florida Flight 90 crashed shortly after taking off from Washington National Airport.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Weather was not the sole cause. NTSB identifies flightcrew anti-ice decisions, takeoff with snow/ice contamination, failure to reject takeoff, and prolonged delay among causes/contributors. Do not present weather alone as causal or use an unsourced casualty figure; contemporaneous airport snowfall reporting/observation windows require independent review.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original two-lane weather-and-deicing timeline matching official NTSB chronology with dated airport weather observations

reviews.title_after: Loma, Montana begins a stunning 103°F warm-up in 24 hours
reviews.evidence_independence: AMS conference abstract presents the NOAA National Climate Extremes Committee's same underlying COOP station and observer review; second URL is not an independent second thermometer
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: On January 14–15, 1972, a weather observer at Loma, Montana recorded a rise from −54°F to 49°F during a 24-hour period as Chinook conditions developed.
reviews.unverified_cautions: The 103°F change spans January 14 into January 15. January 14 begins the episode, not the date the full increase was completed. This is a 24-hour increase, not a two-minute temperature jump like Spearfish in 1943; station siting, calibration, time basis, and current record status need publication-stage review.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original 24-hour chronological COOP thermometer reconstruction with mountain downslope/chinook schematic and source-based time labels

reviews.title_after: Snow flurries reach Miami during the extraordinary January 1977 cold wave
reviews.location_after: Miami–Fort Lauderdale–West Palm Beach, South Florida
reviews.evidence_independence: NWS historical reconstruction and contemporaneous news reporting are different institutions, though both reflect weather observers/eyewitnesses from the same day
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: On January 19, 1977, snow flurries were reported in South Florida as far south as the Miami area and Homestead during an extraordinary cold-air outbreak.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Miami International Airport's official station record did not directly register the snow; reports are supported by widespread eyewitness observations and NWS historical account. Do not claim accumulating snow at Miami airport or imply snowfall throughout all of Florida; compare trace/flurry reports carefully.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original South Florida snow-report footprint with separately classified observation/eyewitness markers and analyzed 850-hPa cold-air intrusion

reviews.title_after: Spearfish, South Dakota warms 49°F in just two minutes
reviews.location_after: Spearfish and Rapid City, Black Hills, South Dakota
reviews.evidence_independence: NWS case-study reproduction of archival recording thermometers and local government commemoration based on the same 1943 measurements; second is not another independent instrument
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: On January 22, 1943, recording thermometers documented Spearfish's temperature rising from −4°F to 45°F in two minutes near an oscillating warm/cold boundary.
reviews.unverified_cautions: The famous 49°F in two minutes is the Spearfish temperature *rise*; the subsequent 58°F temperature fall took 27 minutes, different interval. Historic station thermograph, not a modern ASOS minute data record; check provenance and rights for scans before reproducing chart.
reviews.graphic_concept: Re-plot the original Spearfish two-minute rise and later 27-minute plunge with annotated frontal oscillations and archive-provenance labels

alternate_reviews.title: Prospect Creek, Alaska records −80°F, the United States' lowest official temperature
alternate_reviews.location: Prospect Creek Camp near Dalton Highway, Alaska
alternate_reviews.second_publisher: University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute
alternate_reviews.evidence_independence: Alaska Climate Research Center tabulation and UAF historical article share the same official cooperative observation, not two independent thermometers
alternate_reviews.corroborated_core_claim: Prospect Creek Camp recorded Alaska's and the United States' lowest official temperature of −80°F on January 23, 1971.
alternate_reviews.unverified_cautions: Not the all-time North American temperature record; it refers to the United States. Original value, instrument calibration and physical station identity should be checked if plotted.

alternate_reviews.title: Browning, Montana completes a 100°F plunge between January 23 and 24
alternate_reviews.evidence_independence: Both accounts derive from the same historical Weather Bureau/COOP documentation; NOAA retrospective provides comparison, not independent second temperature measurements
alternate_reviews.corroborated_core_claim: The Browning, Montana 1916 cold-front episode spans January 23–24, when historical records document a 100°F drop from 44°F to −56°F.
alternate_reviews.unverified_cautions: The full decline spanned the two days; February or modern date assumptions are wrong. Loma's 103°F 1972 *rise* later superseded Browning's 100°F 24-hour national change figure. These are opposite-sign events; do not call the 1916 change current national 24-hour record.
